missions.title: Create a named record

lesson.heading: The idea
lesson.text: A dictionary maps keys to values. A literal uses braces and `key: value` pairs. Reading `record["name"]` retrieves the value under that key, not a numeric position. These first records use string keys.

missions.brief: Return a device record with named fields.
requirements: name and `category` are strings. Return a dictionary with exactly the keys `"name"` and `"category"`, holding the supplied values unchanged.
Return the result without printing or reading input inside the helper.
hints: Keys describe what a value means.
The required field names are literal strings, not variable names.
A dictionary literal can directly express this small record.

missions.title: Look up missing stock

lesson.heading: The idea
lesson.text: `dict.get(key, default)` returns a stored value when the key exists, otherwise the default. It does not insert the default into the dictionary. With no explicit default, it returns `None` for missing keys.

missions.brief: Return the stock quantity for name, using zero when that `name` is absent.
requirements: `stock` is a dictionary of string names to non-negative integer quantities; `name` is a string. Preserve the dictionary, including when a lookup misses.
Return the result without printing or reading input inside the helper.
hints: Does the lookup have a sensible answer when no record exists?
Returning a fallback should not create a stock entry.
get can provide a lookup default without a separate insertion.

missions.title: Update the real inventory

lesson.heading: The idea
lesson.text: Assignment to `dictionary[key]` adds or replaces that key's value in place. Existing unrelated keys remain. Like list mutation, the caller sees the changed object.

missions.brief: Store quantity under name in the supplied stock dictionary.
requirements: `stock` maps strings to non-negative integers. `name` is a string and `quantity` is a non-negative integer. Add a missing name or replace its quantity without changing any other entry.
Return `None`; the helper prints nothing. Checks verify the updated input dictionary as well as the return.
missions.example:
set_stock({'A': 1}, 'A', 4) -> None; arguments afterward: [{'A': 4}, 'A', 4]
set_stock({}, 'B', 0) -> None; arguments afterward: [{'B': 0}, 'B', 0]
hints: The caller needs its existing dictionary updated.
An assignment to a key affects one entry, not the whole mapping.
Rebinding stock to a new local dictionary would not fulfill the mutation contract.

missions.title: Present is not the same as nonempty
missions.concepts: Dictionary membership - keys with `None` or zero

lesson.heading: The idea
lesson.text: `key in dictionary` checks whether the key exists. It does not check the stored value's truth value. A field can be present with `None`, `0`, `False` or empty text.

missions.brief: Return whether `record` contains field as a key.
requirements: `record` is a dictionary with string keys and `field` is a string. A present key counts regardless of its value. Do not modify `record`. Return a Boolean.
Return the result without printing or reading input inside the helper.
hints: The question concerns the key, not whether its value looks useful.
A get result of `None` can mean two different things.
Dictionary membership directly answers whether the key exists.

missions.title: Total all quantities

lesson.heading: The idea
lesson.text: Iterating a dictionary directly gives keys. `values()` supplies its values. Use the view that matches the information needed; a total does not need the associated names.

missions.brief: Return the sum of all quantities in stock.
requirements: `stock` maps string names to non-negative integers. Empty stock totals zero. Do not change the dictionary.
Return the result without printing or reading input inside the helper.
hints: The total needs quantities rather than names.
A dictionary loop without a view gives keys.
An accumulator over values works; `sum(stock.values())` is a concise alternative.

missions.title: Find low-stock names

lesson.heading: The idea
lesson.text: `items()` supplies key/value pairs. A loop can unpack each pair into two names, like `enumerate`. Dictionaries preserve insertion order, so iteration can return names in that order.

missions.brief: Return the names whose `stock` is strictly below threshold.
requirements: `stock` maps strings to non-negative integers; `threshold` is a non-negative integer. Return a list of qualifying names in dictionary insertion order, without changing stock. Equality does not qualify.
Return the result without printing or reading input inside the helper.
hints: You need a value for the decision and a key for the output.
items supplies both at once.
Keep the dictionary's iteration order rather than sorting the result.

missions.title: Count repeated words

lesson.heading: The idea
lesson.text: A dictionary can accumulate a separate count for each distinct key. The first occurrence needs an initial count; later occurrences update it. This is the same accumulator idea applied per key.

requirements: `words` is a list of strings. Count exact text, case-sensitively, including empty strings. Empty input returns an empty dictionary. Do not modify `words`.
Return the result without printing or reading input inside the helper.
hints: Each word needs its own accumulator.

missions.title: Find one device record

lesson.heading: The idea
lesson.text: A list of records separates order from named fields. A loop visits each dictionary, then key lookup reads the field needed for a decision. An early return naturally selects the first match.

missions.brief: Return the first device record whose name field equals `name`, or `None` when absent.
requirements: `records` is a list of dictionaries, each containing a string `"name"` field. Other fields may vary and must be retained in the returned record.
Matching is case-sensitive. Preserve the input list and every record. Return the first match if names repeat. A copied matching record is also acceptable.
Return the result without printing or reading input inside the helper.
hints: Inspect one record at a time.
Return the whole matching record, not only its name.
Only `return None` after all candidates have been considered.

missions.title: Remove an optional device

lesson.heading: The idea
lesson.text: `dict.pop(key, default)` removes a present key and returns its old value. When the key is absent it returns the default without changing anything. Unlike `list.pop`, its argument identifies a key rather than an index.

missions.brief: Remove name from `devices` and return its stored location, or `None` if absent.
requirements: `devices` maps string device names to string locations. Change only the requested entry; keep other entries. Return an empty string if that was the stored location.
The helper prints nothing. Checks verify the remaining mapping as well as the returned value.
missions.example:
remove_device({'A': 'Desk', 'B': 'Shelf'}, 'A') -> 'Desk'; arguments afterward: [{'B': 'Shelf'}, 'A']
remove_device({}, 'A') -> None; arguments afterward: [{}, 'A']
hints: Removing and returning a stored value is one dictionary operation.
The missing-key fallback avoids a `KeyError`.
A stored empty string is a real result, not a missing entry.

missions.title: Build an inventory summary
missions.concepts: Chapter project - filtering records and aggregation

lesson.heading: The idea
lesson.text: A small inventory combines the collection techniques you have practiced: named fields, record filtering and totals. A report dictionary lets other code choose how to display the result later.

missions.brief: Return a structured summary of the records in one category.
requirements: Each record has a string `"name"`, string `"category"`, and non-negative integer `"quantity"`. category matching is case-sensitive. Extra record fields should not affect the result.

Return exactly `{"items": N, "units": T, "names": [...]}`. N is the number of matching records, T is their quantity sum, and names is their name list in input order, including duplicate names and zero-quantity records.
No matches means `{"items": 0, "units": 0, "names": []}`. Do not change any input record or the original list.
Return the result without printing or reading input inside the helper.
hints: Apply the category rule consistently to every part of the summary.
Record count and unit count are different quantities.
The names collection also supplies the number of matching records, while a separate accumulator tracks units.
